paragraphs: In Chesterfield, the borough council looks after bins, council tax and housing, while Derbyshire County Council is responsible for social care. That makes the county's fostering service the council option for people living in and around the town, alongside the independent agencies shown above. Derbyshire recruits through Foster for East Midlands, a regional hub that takes first enquiries and supports people through the process.

Derbyshire says it needs foster carers for children of every age and ability, including disabled children and brothers and sisters who need to stay together, and that more carers are urgently needed so children can stay near their schools, friends and communities. The council's own carer stories, published in September 2026, show the range of the role: caring for babies and toddlers, offering regular weekend short breaks, and looking after children for six to 18 months while longer-term plans are made. Its looked-after children's sufficiency strategy for 2017 to 2021 found that the number of children in its care grew fastest among those under ten between 2018 and 2020.

The county asks only that you are 21 or over and have a spare room; no qualifications are needed. Single people, couples, gay, straight and trans people, renters and homeowners, and people who work or do not work can all apply. Carers receive training, guidance and ongoing support, and the council runs drop-in events where you can talk to people who already foster.

Every fostering service in England must pay at least the national minimum allowance. Outside London and the South East, for 2026-27 that is £176 a week for a child aged 0 to 2, £182 for 3 to 4, £201 for 5 to 10, £227 for 11 to 15 and £267 for 16 to 17. Many services add a fee for the carer, so ask the council and two or three of the agencies above what they pay and how they support carers.
